SUNDIAL ENGINEERING & SURVEY

4720 South Rainbow Boulevard, Suite 210  •  Las Vegas, Nevada 89103  •  (702) 555-0142  •  NV COA #C-3874

MEMORANDUM

1. Bottom line

You asked whether the emergency spillway as drawn on C-9 holds up, whether G-4 can be answered from the current sheet, whether the correction triggers an amendment to the accepted Master Drainage Study, what the revised C-9 detail and basin notes must say, and where the overflow goes. Our answers are:

Answer 1 — G-4. The spillway as drawn does not hold up, and G-4 cannot be answered from C-9 as issued on 08/21/2026. The sheet shows a 20-ft-wide broad-crested weir but gives no design flow, no sizing calculation, no spillway section or freeboard dimension from the spillway design water surface, and no designed apron. At the accepted Phase 3 inflow of 88.4 cfs with the principal outlet blocked, the 20-ft weir requires 1.294793994 ft of head; only 0.70 ft is available between crest 2,858.50 ft and top of berm 2,859.20 ft. The design water surface is 2,859.794793994 ft, which overtops the berm by 0.594793994 ft. Even crediting the 41.5 cfs outlet discharge at the crest, the spillway would still overtop by 0.148557080 ft. The existing 15 ft by 20 ft grouted riprap apron with D50 = 12 in is also undersized for the calculated toe velocity of about 19.53 ft/s.

Answer 2 — Amendment. No formal amendment to the accepted Master Drainage Study is required for the G-4 correction. The 100-year water surface at 2,857.91 ft, the Phase 3 allocation of 6.4 acre-feet, the 40.0-acre/42% tributary basis, the Parcel E basin location, and the 78 cfs shared-outfall cap do not change. The correction is a plan-level C-6/C-9 detail. Because the top of berm moves from 2,859.20 ft to 2,860.80 ft, we will transmit the revised C-9 and spillway calculation to CCRFCD for concurrence under Condition 2 of the tentative map; that is a district concurrence, not a new hydrology study or an MDS amendment.

Answer 3 — Revised C-9. The revised C-9 must show a 36-ft minimum broad-crested weir at crest 2,858.50 ft, design Q = 88.4 cfs, head 0.875022069 ft, design WSE 2,859.375022069 ft, top of berm 2,860.80 ft, freeboard 1.424977931 ft at Q100 and 1.153396722 ft at 1.5Q = 132.6 cfs. The crest and chute should be 12 in by 18 in articulated concrete block over geotextile with cutoff walls, followed by a reinforced concrete stilling basin at least 20 ft long by 36 ft wide by 12 in thick with baffle blocks and an end sill, then 18-in D50 riprap at 27 in thick for 10 ft. The basin notes must correct the crest offset to 0.59 ft, state the design flow and spillway freeboard, and retain the 6.4 acre-feet allocation and the MDS reference.

Answer 4 — Overflow. Overflow leaves the east berm, crosses Common-Area Parcel E in an open swale to the Windmill Lane gutter line, and must then run west along Windmill Lane to the shared outfall at the southwest corner and the CCRFCD regional facility. The current record does not show a continuous swale alignment or inverts, a gutter capacity check, or a drainage easement. The revised C-9 must show the path wholly within Parcel E and public right-of-way, or add a drainage easement, and must demonstrate capacity. The emergency overflow is not routed through the 30-in principal outlet pipe.

2. Purpose, records and governing basis

This memorandum is the engineering record of our review of the C-9 emergency spillway against the accepted Master Drainage Study (MDS), the Phase 3 improvement plans, the storm drain worksheets, the Phase 2 comments and the Clark County Regional Flood Control District (CCRFCD) acceptance letter. It answers CCPW comment G-4 in advance of assigning the detailed C-9 revision to the drainage lead. It does not replace the revised C-9, the spillway calculation sheet, or the CCRFCD concurrence.

The records relied on are listed below. Record abbreviations used in the rest of the memo are shown in brackets.

3. Can G-4 be answered with what is on C-9 today?

No. C-9 as issued on 08/21/2026 identifies an emergency spillway and gives a few dimensions, but it does not contain the engineering content that G-4 requests. Specifically, the sheet does not give a design flow, a weir sizing calculation, a spillway section with headwater and tailwater, a freeboard dimension measured from the spillway design water surface, or an apron/erosion-protection design. The QA/QC checklist's statement that the weir detail is complete is incorrect (Section 9).

Table 3-1 lists what the sheet actually says. The values are taken directly from C-9 pages 17 and 18 and C-6 page 11.

Table 3-1 — Existing C-9 spillway data.

The 1.29 ft dimension in the basin notes is a 100-year-event freeboard, and it is correct as far as it goes. It is not the spillway freeboard. Because the crest is only 0.70 ft below the top of berm, any spillway flow consumes that 0.70 ft at a one-to-one rate. At the design flow the spillway design water surface is above the top of berm. A note that says the basin has 1.29 ft of freeboard at the 100-year water surface does not answer G-4 and does not make the spillway adequate.

The current C-9 should not be submitted as the G-4 response. A note-only response will not close G-4. The drainage lead must revise the spillway detail, section, apron and basin notes and prepare the calculation; the minimum content is set out in Sections 5 and 6.

4. Spillway sizing — the 20-ft weir does not pass the design flow

4.1 Design basis

The design storm for peak flow is the 100-year, 6-hour storm with a rainfall depth of 2.38 in (MDS Section 3.1, p.4, and Appendix A, p.10). The 100-year, 24-hour depth of 3.18 in governs detention storage volume, not peak spillway flow (MDS Section 4.2, p.6). The Phase 3 routed peak inflow to the shared detention basin is 88.4 cfs (MDS Appendix C, Table C-2, p.12; HYD Peak Flows, cell B13).

The arithmetic sum of the four Phase 3 sub-basin peaks is 96.8 cfs; after accounting for timing along the Phase 3 trunk, the combined inflow at the basin is 88.4 cfs (HYD Peak Flows, cells B12 and B13; MDS Appendix C, Table C-2, p.12).

The emergency spillway design flow is 88.4 cfs with the principal outlet assumed fully blocked. This is the conservative CCRFCD detention-basin check: the spillway must pass the unrouted 100-year inflow without credit for the outlet. We also checked 1.5 times the design flow, 132.6 cfs, so the selected geometry has reserve if the District requires a 1.5Q spillway check. Using the routed outflow of 27.9 cfs (MDS Appendix D-1, p.13) as the spillway design flow would under-size the spillway and is not accepted.

The current RFCD Hydrologic Criteria and Drainage Design Manual text is not included in the record set provided for this review. The calculation therefore applies the conservative standard detention-basin check—100-year peak inflow with the outlet blocked—and also checks 1.5Q. The CCRFCD concurrence transmittal will confirm the current manual criterion; the selected geometry passes both Q100 and 1.5Q, so a more stringent criterion up to 1.5Q does not change the C-9 geometry.

The weir is a broad-crested weir. In U.S. customary units:

Q = C · L · H^(3/2)

H = (Q / (C · L))^(2/3)

where Q is discharge in cubic feet per second, C is the broad-crested weir coefficient in ft^0.5/s, L is the crest length in feet, and H is the head above the crest in feet. We use C = 3.0 ft^0.5/s for a broad-crested concrete/articulated-block crest and check C = 2.6 ft^0.5/s as a conservative sensitivity. No intermediate value is rounded in the calculations below.

4.2 Existing 20-ft weir at crest 2,858.50 ft

With L = 20 ft and C = 3.0 ft^0.5/s:

H = (88.4 / (3.0 × 20))^(2/3) = (88.4 / 60)^(2/3) = 1.294793994 ft

Design WSE = 2,858.50 + 1.294793994 = 2,859.794793994 ft

Available head to top of berm = 2,859.20 − 2,858.50 = 0.70 ft

Overtopping = 2,859.794793994 − 2,859.20 = 0.594793994 ft

The capacity of the 20-ft weir at the available 0.70 ft head is:

Q = 3.0 × 20 × (0.70)^(3/2) = 35.139721114 cfs

With the conservative C = 2.6 ft^0.5/s, the required head is 1.424402129 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.924402129 ft, and the overtopping is 0.724402129 ft. The capacity at 0.70 ft is 30.454424966 cfs. The crest length required to pass 88.4 cfs at 0.70 ft is 50.313432888 ft with C = 3.0, or 58.053961025 ft with C = 2.6. The 20-ft weir is less than half the required length. At a 50.313432888-ft length the design WSE would equal the existing top of berm at 2,859.20 ft, leaving zero freeboard; crest length alone does not solve the problem.

Even if the outlet is credited at the crest, the check still fails. MDS Appendix D-2 gives 41.5 cfs outflow at elevation 2,858.50 ft. The spillway would then need to pass 88.4 − 41.5 = 46.9 cfs:

H = (46.9 / (3.0 × 20))^(2/3) = 0.848557080 ft

Design WSE = 2,858.50 + 0.848557080 = 2,859.348557080 ft

Overtopping = 2,859.348557080 − 2,859.20 = 0.148557080 ft

With C = 2.6, the credited-outlet head is 0.933497156 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.433497156 ft, and the overtopping is 0.233497156 ft. This is a conservative fixed-outlet credit at the crest; a coupled outlet/spillway rating would lower the water surface slightly as the outlet head rises, but it would not restore the 1.0-ft freeboard because the crest is only 0.70 ft below the top of berm. The conclusion is the same under either reading: the 20-ft spillway cannot pass the 100-year inflow within the available berm height, and it cannot provide the required freeboard.

4.3 Required geometry for the revised C-9

The crest elevation of 2,858.50 ft is retained because it is 0.59 ft above the accepted 100-year water surface of 2,857.91 ft and is fixed in MDS Appendix D-2. The crest length is increased to 36 ft and the top of berm is raised to 2,860.80 ft. The 36-ft length is a practical multiple of the 18-in articulated-block width (24 blocks) and fits along the 195-ft east berm (C-6, p.11). It is selected for reserve: a 30-ft weir would give 1.005206005 ft freeboard at 1.5Q (utilisation 0.995), while 36 ft gives 1.153396722 ft (utilisation 0.867); a longer weir would add crest and basin width without a corresponding benefit. The calculations are:

H at Q100 = (88.4 / (3.0 × 36))^(2/3) = 0.875022069 ft

Design WSE at Q100 = 2,858.50 + 0.875022069 = 2,859.375022069 ft

H at 1.5Q = (132.6 / (3.0 × 36))^(2/3) = 1.146603278 ft

Design WSE at 1.5Q = 2,858.50 + 1.146603278 = 2,859.646603278 ft

Freeboard at Q100 = 2,860.80 − 2,859.375022069 = 1.424977931 ft

Freeboard at 1.5Q = 2,860.80 − 2,859.646603278 = 1.153396722 ft

The conservative C = 2.6 check also passes: at Q100 the head is 0.962611275 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.462611275 ft, and the freeboard is 1.337388725 ft; at 1.5Q the head is 1.261377607 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.761377607 ft, and the freeboard is 1.038622393 ft. The 100-year freeboard to the new top of berm is 2,860.80 − 2,857.91 = 2.89 ft, and the crest-to-top dimension is 2,860.80 − 2,858.50 = 2.30 ft. Widening the weir alone is not sufficient: at Q100 the 36-ft design WSE of 2,859.375022069 ft is above the existing top of berm of 2,859.20 ft, so the top of berm must be raised to provide freeboard.

Table 4-1 — Spillway elevation stack (all elevations NAVD 88).

Table 4-2 — Spillway capacity and freeboard check. The table shows final values rounded to four decimal places; the unrounded values are in the calculation text above.

For completeness, the 36-ft weir also passes the arithmetic sum of the Phase 3 sub-basin peaks, 96.8 cfs: the head is 0.929610602 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.429610602 ft, and the freeboard to 2,860.80 ft is 1.370389398 ft. The 88.4 cfs timing-adjusted inflow remains the design basis.

Raising the top of berm by 1.60 ft is feasible within Parcel E. C-6 gives the basin top-of-berm footprint as approximately 293 ft by 195 ft, or 1.31 acres (C-6, p.11). The final map gives Parcel E as 2.04 acres (Final map, Sheet 4, 08/21/2026). With 4H:1V interior and 3H:1V exterior slopes, the top-of-berm footprint expands by roughly 0.15 acre, to about 1.46 acres, which remains inside the 2.04-acre parcel. The berm raise itself fits; the stilling basin, 10-ft riprap and overflow swale must also be shown inside Parcel E or within a drainage easement. The current C-6 does not dimension the east berm margin, so the revised C-6/C-9 must confirm that the 20-ft basin, the riprap and the swale fit. If they do not, the spillway must be shifted or an easement obtained; the basin and swale cannot be built outside Parcel E without an easement. All top-of-berm appurtenances must be raised with the berm, including the outlet headwall (currently top at 2,859.20 ft on C-9, p.18), the access gate and the perimeter maintenance path.

4.4 Apron and erosion protection

The existing apron is 15 ft by 20 ft of grouted riprap with D50 = 12 in (C-9, p.17). It has no velocity basis. Using the existing 20-ft weir, the unit discharge at Q100 is 88.4/20 = 4.42 cfs/ft; critical depth is 0.846570029 ft and critical velocity is 5.221068370 ft/s. With a 5.5-ft drop from crest 2,858.50 ft to natural grade 2,853.00 ft, the ideal toe velocity is about 19.530989604 ft/s. For the proposed 36-ft weir, the unit discharge is 2.455555556 cfs/ft, critical depth is 0.572112213 ft, critical velocity is 4.292087285 ft/s, and the toe velocity is still about 19.303419730 ft/s because the drop dominates.

The Isbash riprap sizing check is:

D50 = V^2 / [2 · g · C^2 · (Gs − 1)]

With V = 19.530989604 ft/s, g = 32.2 ft/s^2, C = 0.86 for high turbulence, and Gs = 2.65, the required D50 is 4.853798953 ft, or 58.25 in. Reversing the equation, a 12-in D50 stone is adequate only to about 8.865094247 ft/s. The calculated toe velocity is more than twice that. A 12-in grouted riprap apron cannot be justified by calculation, and increasing the stone to a practical size is not the right solution at this drop. The revised C-9 must use a reinforced concrete stilling basin.

The minimum acceptable detail is a reinforced concrete stilling basin at least 20 ft long by 36 ft wide, 12 in thick, with baffle blocks and an end sill, keyed 3 ft below grade with cutoff walls at the upstream and downstream ends and weep holes. Downstream of the basin, provide riprap with D50 = 18 in, thickness 27 in (1.5 times D50), 10 ft long by 36 ft wide, over a geotextile filter fabric, keyed into the toe. The drainage lead must demonstrate by calculation that the basin reduces the exit velocity to the riprap allowable velocity; the 18-in D50 is a minimum, not a substitute for the basin design.

5. What the revised C-9 spillway detail must say

The revised C-9 must replace the current bullet-list detail with a dimensioned spillway plan and section. The following table is the minimum content. Each value is to be shown on the drawing and tied to the calculation sheet.

The spillway section must show the upstream and downstream water surfaces, the head H above the crest, the design WSE, the top of berm and the freeboard dimension. It must also show the existing ground at the toe (2,853.00 ft), the stilling basin, the cutoff walls, the riprap and the geotextile. A bullet list without dimensions does not satisfy G-4.

6. What the revised C-9 basin notes must say

The current basin notes contain a correct 100-year freeboard statement (1.29 ft) but an incorrect crest offset and no spillway design basis. The notes say the crest is 0.60 ft above the 100-year water surface; the detail says 0.71 ft; the arithmetic is 0.59 ft. The revised notes must replace both numbers with 0.59 ft and must state the spillway design flow, design WSE and freeboard. The following note text is to be carried on revised C-9, with the values shown in the table above.

The revised notes must not repeat the current 0.60 ft or 0.71 ft crest offset. They must not describe the 100-year freeboard of 1.29 ft as the spillway freeboard. They must not use the 100-year, 24-hour storm as the spillway design flow; that storm governs storage volume, not peak spillway discharge.

7. Where the overflow goes once it leaves the berm

The intended overflow path in the current record is: east berm emergency spillway → open swale in Common-Area Parcel E → Windmill Lane gutter line (C-9, Emergency Spillway Detail, p.17). From the Windmill Lane gutter line, the only receiving point of record is the shared outfall at the southwest corner of the parent parcel. The site slopes from the northeast at about 2,905 ft to the southwest outfall at about 2,850 ft (MDS Sections 2.1 and 2.4, p.3–4). The basin outlet is the existing 30-in RCP stub at the southwest corner with invert 2,850.75 ft (C-6, p.11; C-9, p.17), which connects to the CCRFCD regional facility (MDS Section 5.1, p.7; FCD acceptance letter, p.2). The overflow therefore must run west along Windmill Lane to that outfall; it cannot run east away from the only identified receiving point.

The current record does not demonstrate that path. C-9 has a note, not a plan or profile. There is no swale centerline, invert, width, slope or capacity; no gutter capacity check; and no drainage easement for the overflow across Parcel E. The final map shows a 15-ft drainage easement along the west line of Parcel D, but no overflow easement for Parcel E (Final map, Sheet 3 and Sheet 4, 08/21/2026). The overflow is also not the 30-in principal outlet; the 30-in RCP is the normal basin outlet, not an emergency spillway conduit. Sending 88.4 cfs through the 30-in outlet would be a different design and is not what C-9 shows.

Our conclusion is that the overflow is intended to end at the shared outfall and the CCRFCD regional facility, but the path is not demonstrated on the current drawings. Until the revised C-9 shows a continuous, positively graded, capacity-checked path within Parcel E and public right-of-way, G-4 cannot be closed. The final map and the drainage narrative must be consistent with that path; if an easement is needed, it must be granted by the final map under Condition 3.

8. Does the G-4 correction trigger an amendment to the accepted Master Drainage Study?

No. The accepted MDS fixes the Phase 3 detention allocation, the 100-year water surface, the tributary breakdown and the shared outfall cap. The G-4 correction changes the spillway crest length, the top of berm and the apron detail on C-6/C-9; it does not change any of the accepted hydrologic or outfall parameters. Table 8-1 compares the accepted basis with the revised C-9.

Table 8-1 — Amendment comparison: accepted MDS basis versus revised C-9.

The MDS amendment triggers are specific. Section 4.4 says any change to the detention allocation — whether by revision of tributary area, impervious assumption, hydrologic methodology or storage-indication input — is a formal amendment. Section 7.3 says changes to the accepted detention allocations, the outfall allowance, or the tributary breakdown and phase boundaries require an amendment. The FCD acceptance letter adds any revision of phase tributary area, impervious cover, hydrologic methodology, storage-indication input, phase boundary, detention basin location, or shared outfall discharge cap. None of those changes is proposed here. The 100-year stage-storage below 2,857.91 ft, which is the storage-indication input for the accepted 100-year routing, is unchanged; the volume added by raising the top of berm is freeboard above the 100-year water surface and does not enter the accepted 100-year routing. Consistent with the June 22, 2026 pre-application notes (Section 3.2), a narrative-level reconciliation is sufficient where the Phase 3 volumes and outfall configuration match the MDS; the revised C-9 and drainage narrative will include that reconciliation.

Two record points need to be kept straight. First, the C-4 through C-7 sub-basin tabulation sums to approximately 42.05 acres, which is 2.05 acres more than the 40.0-acre Phase 3 parcel. The C-4 note explains that the excess is adjacent half-width right-of-way

5.3 Interpretation
Measured infiltration rates in the shallow silty sand horizon (1.8 to 6.2 in/hr) are considered favorable for basin
infiltration and would support surface retention/infiltration basin design where the basin invert is established
either above the caliche horizon or where any indurated caliche crust encountered at the invert is
over-excavated (typically 12 to 24 inches) and replaced with clean, well-graded select granular material
(sand-and-gravel mixture with less than 10% fines).
Cemented caliche encountered at INF-4 is largely impermeable (0.2 in/hr) and is a limiting layer where present
at the invert. For final drainage design, we recommend a factor of safety of 2 applied to the field-measured
infiltration rate consistent with Clark County Regional Flood Control District guidance for infiltration-supported
detention/retention.
Complete infiltration test data sheets are provided in Appendix C.

construction.
6.2 Site Preparation and Earthwork
Strip and remove all surface vegetation, root mats, debris and any topsoil pockets. Anticipated stripping
depth is generally less than 6 inches across the site.
Following stripping, the exposed subgrade shall be scarified to a depth of 8 inches, moisture-conditioned to
within ±2% of optimum moisture content, and compacted to a minimum of 95% of the maximum dry density
determined by ASTM D1557.
Engineered fill shall be placed in lifts not exceeding 8 inches loose thickness, moisture-conditioned, and
compacted to a minimum of 95% of the ASTM D1557 maximum dry density.
On-site native soils, free of oversized materials (particles greater than 4 inches in maximum dimension) and
organics, are suitable for reuse as engineered fill.
Over-excavation of localized caliche crust may be required at grade transitions to establish a uniform
subgrade support condition, particularly under building pads and pavements. Where cuts expose caliche
within 12 inches of finished subgrade, we recommend over-excavation to at least 24 inches below finished
subgrade and replacement with properly compacted engineered fill.
6.3 Foundation Recommendations
Conventional continuous and isolated spread footings founded on a minimum of 24 inches of properly
compacted engineered fill, or on native soils prepared as described above, are recommended for support of the
single-family residential structures.

• Allowable bearing pressure: 2,500 psf for dead-plus-live loads, increaseable by one-third for transient
loads (wind, seismic).
• Minimum footing width: 12 inches (continuous), 24 inches (isolated).
• Minimum embedment: 18 inches below lowest adjacent finished grade.
• Estimated total settlement: less than 1 inch; differential settlement less than ½ inch between adjacent
footings.
• Lateral resistance: coefficient of friction µ = 0.40 between footing base and compacted engineered fill;
allowable passive equivalent fluid pressure = 300 pcf against footing sides and grade beams, neglecting the
upper 12 inches.
Because the surficial soils are non-expansive (Section 4.4), post-tensioned slab-on-ground foundations are not

# Asks — direct answers and where they appear in the memo

1. **Can G-4 be answered with what is on C-9 today?**
   No. C-9 has no spillway sizing calculation, no spillway section/freeboard dimension from the spillway design WSE, and no apron/erosion design. The 20-ft x 6-ft broad-crested weir is undersized: at the 100-yr Phase 3 inflow of 88.4 cfs with the outlet blocked, required head is 1.2948 ft but only 0.70 ft is available to top of berm; it overtops the berm by 0.5948 ft. See memo §3 and §4.

2. **Does the G-4 revision trigger an amendment to the accepted master drainage study?**
   No formal MDS amendment is triggered by the spillway correction, provided the 100-yr WSE 2,857.91 ft, the 6.4 ac-ft Phase 3 allocation, the 40.0 ac/42% tributary basis, the Parcel E basin location, and the 78 cfs shared-outfall cap remain unchanged. The correction is a plan-level C-6/C-9 detail. Because the top of berm moves from 2,859.20 ft to 2,860.80 ft, transmit the revised C-9/spillway calculation to CCRFCD for concurrence under Condition 2; that is not a new hydrology study or amendment. See memo §7.

3. **What must the spillway detail and basin notes say on the revised C-9?**
   Spillway crest 2,858.50 ft (0.59 ft above 100-yr WSE 2,857.91 ft, not 0.60 or 0.71); design flow 88.4 cfs with outlet blocked; 1.5Q check 132.6 cfs; minimum 36-ft broad-crested weir, C = 3.0, head 0.875 ft at Q100; top of berm 2,860.80 ft; freeboard 1.425 ft at Q100 and 1.153 ft at 1.5Q (C = 2.6 also passes); 12-in x 18-in ACB crest, cutoff walls; reinforced concrete stilling basin at least 20 ft x 36 ft x 12 in with baffle blocks/end sill and 3-ft cutoff; downstream riprap D50 18 in, 27 in thick, 10 ft. Basin notes must state the design flow, spillway design WSE and freeboard, the 6.4 ac-ft allocation/provided volume, and the MDS reference. The RFCD manual text itself is not in the record set; the memo applies the conservative 100-year blocked-outlet check and a 1.5Q check and confirms both. See memo §4, §5 and §6.

4. **Where does the overflow end up once it leaves the berm?**
   East berm spillway -> open swale in Common-Area Parcel E -> Windmill Lane gutter line -> west along Windmill Lane to the shared outfall at the southwest corner -> CCRFCD regional facility. The current C-9 does not show a continuous swale alignment/inverts, capacity check or drainage easement; the revised C-9 must show the path wholly within Parcel E/public ROW or add a drainage easement. The overflow is not routed through the 30-in principal outlet pipe. See memo §6.

5. **Work against the improvement plans and QA/QC checklist.**
   Done. C-1, C-6 and C-9 values checked; QA/QC Tab 3 is wrong to certify Detail 4 as complete and mislabels Section A-A as typical and Section B-B as the outlet swale (A-A is longitudinal through the outlet; B-B is transverse). See memo §2 and §8.

6. **Work against the master drainage study and storm drain worksheets.**
   Done. MDS Rev 1 Feb 2022 Table 4-1, Appendix C, Appendix D-2; Storm Drain HGL July 2026 Inputs/HGL Summary. Spillway design flow 88.4 cfs and 100-yr WSE 2,857.91 ft confirmed. See memo §2 and §3.

7. **Work against the Phase 2 comments and FCD acceptance letter.**
   Done. Phase 2 G-3 freeboard 1.0 ft requirement and G-2 outlet-detail reconciliation are carried; FCD 2/28/2022 amendment triggers are applied. See memo §2 and §7. CCRFCD concurrence is the schedule-critical item; memo §10 sets 11/18/2026 transmittal and a 11/25/2026 fallback so the 11/30/2026 resubmittal is not held.

8. **Memo to Callaway for signature, dated 10/31/2026.**
   Delivered at `/filesystem/Memo_to_Callaway_Spillway_2026-10-31.docx`, addressed to Garrett Nokes, Callaway Land Partners, with signature block for Max Braddock, PM.

9. **Commit to one disposition on each question.**
   Memo gives one disposition per question; no alternatives presented as choices.

10. **Units on every value and name the record.**
    Every value in the memo carries units and a record citation (document, section/table/page/date). See memo tables and footnotes.

11. **Do not round intermediate values.**
    Calculations show full precision intermediate values; final values rounded only for presentation.

12. **Professional engineering standards.**
    Memo applies CCRFCD detention/spillway practice, broad-crested weir hydraulics, Isbash riprap check, geotechnical subgrade preparation and engineered-fill compaction (8-in scarify/lifts, 95% ASTM D1557) for the 1.60-ft berm raise, and clearly separates the accepted design basis from preliminary/non-adopted records. See memo §4.3 and §10.

[0](Normal) SUNDIAL ENGINEERING & SURVEY
[1](Normal) 4720 South Rainbow Boulevard, Suite 210  •  Las Vegas, Nevada 89103  •  (702) 555-0142  •  NV COA #C-3874
[2](Normal) MEMORANDUM
[4](Heading 1) 1. Bottom line
[5](Normal) You asked whether the emergency spillway as drawn on C-9 holds up, whether G-4 can be answered from the current sheet, whether the correction triggers an amendment to the accepted Master Drainage Study, what the revised C-9 detail and basin notes must say, and where the overflow goes. Our answers are:
[6](List Bullet) Answer 1 — G-4. The spillway as drawn does not hold up, and G-4 cannot be answered from C-9 as issued on 08/21/2026. The sheet shows a 20-ft-wide broad-crested weir but gives no design flow, no sizing calculation, no spillway section or freeboard dimension from the spillway design water surface, and no designed apron. At the accepted Phase 3 inflow of 88.4 cfs with the principal outlet blocked, the 20-ft weir requires 1.294793994 ft of head; only 0.70 ft is available between crest 2,858.50 ft and top of berm 2,859.20 ft. The design water surface is 2,859.794793994 ft, which overtops the berm by 0.594793994 ft. Even crediting the 41.5 cfs outlet discharge at the crest, the spillway would still overtop by 0.148557080 ft. The existing 15 ft by 20 ft grouted riprap apron with D50 = 12 in is also undersized for the calculated toe velocity of about 19.53 ft/s.
[7](List Bullet) Answer 2 — Amendment. No formal amendment to the accepted Master Drainage Study is required for the G-4 correction. The 100-year water surface at 2,857.91 ft, the Phase 3 allocation of 6.4 acre-feet, the 40.0-acre/42% tributary basis, the Parcel E basin location, and the 78 cfs shared-outfall cap do not change. The correction is a plan-level C-6/C-9 detail. Because the top of berm moves from 2,859.20 ft to 2,860.80 ft, we will transmit the revised C-9 and spillway calculation to CCRFCD for concurrence under Condition 2 of the tentative map; that is a district concurrence, not a new hydrology study or an MDS amendment.
[8](List Bullet) Answer 3 — Revised C-9. The revised C-9 must show a 36-ft minimum broad-crested weir at crest 2,858.50 ft, design Q = 88.4 cfs, head 0.875022069 ft, design WSE 2,859.375022069 ft, top of berm 2,860.80 ft, freeboard 1.424977931 ft at Q100 and 1.153396722 ft at 1.5Q = 132.6 cfs. The crest and chute should be 12 in by 18 in articulated concrete block over geotextile with cutoff walls, followed by a reinforced concrete stilling basin at least 20 ft long by 36 ft wide by 12 in thick with baffle blocks and an end sill, then 18-in D50 riprap at 27 in thick for 10 ft. The basin notes must correct the crest offset to 0.59 ft, state the design flow and spillway freeboard, and retain the 6.4 acre-feet allocation and the MDS reference.
[9](List Bullet) Answer 4 — Overflow. Overflow leaves the east berm, crosses Common-Area Parcel E in an open swale to the Windmill Lane gutter line, and must then run west along Windmill Lane to the shared outfall at the southwest corner and the CCRFCD regional facility. The current record does not show a continuous swale alignment or inverts, a gutter capacity check, or a drainage easement. The revised C-9 must show the path wholly within Parcel E and public right-of-way, or add a drainage easement, and must demonstrate capacity. The emergency overflow is not routed through the 30-in principal outlet pipe.
[10](Heading 1) 2. Purpose, records and governing basis
[11](Normal) This memorandum is the engineering record of our review of the C-9 emergency spillway against the accepted Master Drainage Study (MDS), the Phase 3 improvement plans, the storm drain worksheets, the Phase 2 comments and the Clark County Regional Flood Control District (CCRFCD) acceptance letter. It answers CCPW comment G-4 in advance of assigning the detailed C-9 revision to the drainage lead. It does not replace the revised C-9, the spillway calculation sheet, or the CCRFCD concurrence.
[12](Normal) The records relied on are listed below. Record abbreviations used in the rest of the memo are shown in brackets.
[15](Heading 1) 3. Can G-4 be answered with what is on C-9 today?
[16](Normal) No. C-9 as issued on 08/21/2026 identifies an emergency spillway and gives a few dimensions, but it does not contain the engineering content that G-4 requests. Specifically, the sheet does not give a design flow, a weir sizing calculation, a spillway section with headwater and tailwater, a freeboard dimension measured from the spillway design water surface, or an apron/erosion-protection design. The QA/QC checklist's statement that the weir detail is complete is incorrect (Section 9).
[17](Normal) Table 3-1 lists what the sheet actually says. The values are taken directly from C-9 pages 17 and 18 and C-6 page 11.
[18](Normal) Table 3-1 — Existing C-9 spillway data.
[20](Normal) The 1.29 ft dimension in the basin notes is a 100-year-event freeboard, and it is correct as far as it goes. It is not the spillway freeboard. Because the crest is only 0.70 ft below the top of berm, any spillway flow consumes that 0.70 ft at a one-to-one rate. At the design flow the spillway design water surface is above the top of berm. A note that says the basin has 1.29 ft of freeboard at the 100-year water surface does not answer G-4 and does not make the spillway adequate.
[21](Normal) The current C-9 should not be submitted as the G-4 response. A note-only response will not close G-4. The drainage lead must revise the spillway detail, section, apron and basin notes and prepare the calculation; the minimum content is set out in Sections 5 and 6.
[22](Heading 1) 4. Spillway sizing — the 20-ft weir does not pass the design flow
[23](Heading 2) 4.1 Design basis
[24](Normal) The design storm for peak flow is the 100-year, 6-hour storm with a rainfall depth of 2.38 in (MDS Section 3.1, p.4, and Appendix A, p.10). The 100-year, 24-hour depth of 3.18 in governs detention storage volume, not peak spillway flow (MDS Section 4.2, p.6). The Phase 3 routed peak inflow to the shared detention basin is 88.4 cfs (MDS Appendix C, Table C-2, p.12; HYD Peak Flows, cell B13).
[25](Normal) The arithmetic sum of the four Phase 3 sub-basin peaks is 96.8 cfs; after accounting for timing along the Phase 3 trunk, the combined inflow at the basin is 88.4 cfs (HYD Peak Flows, cells B12 and B13; MDS Appendix C, Table C-2, p.12).
[26](Normal) The emergency spillway design flow is 88.4 cfs with the principal outlet assumed fully blocked. This is the conservative CCRFCD detention-basin check: the spillway must pass the unrouted 100-year inflow without credit for the outlet. We also checked 1.5 times the design flow, 132.6 cfs, so the selected geometry has reserve if the District requires a 1.5Q spillway check. Using the routed outflow of 27.9 cfs (MDS Appendix D-1, p.13) as the spillway design flow would under-size the spillway and is not accepted.
[27](Normal) The current RFCD Hydrologic Criteria and Drainage Design Manual text is not included in the record set provided for this review. The calculation therefore applies the conservative standard detention-basin check—100-year peak inflow with the outlet blocked—and also checks 1.5Q. The CCRFCD concurrence transmittal will confirm the current manual criterion; the selected geometry passes both Q100 and 1.5Q, so a more stringent criterion up to 1.5Q does not change the C-9 geometry.
[28](Normal) The weir is a broad-crested weir. In U.S. customary units:
[29](Normal) Q = C · L · H^(3/2)
[30](Normal) H = (Q / (C · L))^(2/3)
[31](Normal) where Q is discharge in cubic feet per second, C is the broad-crested weir coefficient in ft^0.5/s, L is the crest length in feet, and H is the head above the crest in feet. We use C = 3.0 ft^0.5/s for a broad-crested concrete/articulated-block crest and check C = 2.6 ft^0.5/s as a conservative sensitivity. No intermediate value is rounded in the calculations below.
[32](Heading 2) 4.2 Existing 20-ft weir at crest 2,858.50 ft
[33](Normal) With L = 20 ft and C = 3.0 ft^0.5/s:
[34](Normal) H = (88.4 / (3.0 × 20))^(2/3) = (88.4 / 60)^(2/3) = 1.294793994 ft
[35](Normal) Design WSE = 2,858.50 + 1.294793994 = 2,859.794793994 ft
[36](Normal) Available head to top of berm = 2,859.20 − 2,858.50 = 0.70 ft
[37](Normal) Overtopping = 2,859.794793994 − 2,859.20 = 0.594793994 ft
[38](Normal) The capacity of the 20-ft weir at the available 0.70 ft head is:
[39](Normal) Q = 3.0 × 20 × (0.70)^(3/2) = 35.139721114 cfs
[40](Normal) With the conservative C = 2.6 ft^0.5/s, the required head is 1.424402129 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.924402129 ft, and the overtopping is 0.724402129 ft. The capacity at 0.70 ft is 30.454424966 cfs. The crest length required to pass 88.4 cfs at 0.70 ft is 50.313432888 ft with C = 3.0, or 58.053961025 ft with C = 2.6. The 20-ft weir is less than half the required length. At a 50.313432888-ft length the design WSE would equal the existing top of berm at 2,859.20 ft, leaving zero freeboard; crest length alone does not solve the problem.
[41](Normal) Even if the outlet is credited at the crest, the check still fails. MDS Appendix D-2 gives 41.5 cfs outflow at elevation 2,858.50 ft. The spillway would then need to pass 88.4 − 41.5 = 46.9 cfs:
[42](Normal) H = (46.9 / (3.0 × 20))^(2/3) = 0.848557080 ft
[43](Normal) Design WSE = 2,858.50 + 0.848557080 = 2,859.348557080 ft
[44](Normal) Overtopping = 2,859.348557080 − 2,859.20 = 0.148557080 ft
[45](Normal) With C = 2.6, the credited-outlet head is 0.933497156 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.433497156 ft, and the overtopping is 0.233497156 ft. This is a conservative fixed-outlet credit at the crest; a coupled outlet/spillway rating would lower the water surface slightly as the outlet head rises, but it would not restore the 1.0-ft freeboard because the crest is only 0.70 ft below the top of berm. The conclusion is the same under either reading: the 20-ft spillway cannot pass the 100-year inflow within the available berm height, and it cannot provide the required freeboard.
[46](Heading 2) 4.3 Required geometry for the revised C-9
[47](Normal) The crest elevation of 2,858.50 ft is retained because it is 0.59 ft above the accepted 100-year water surface of 2,857.91 ft and is fixed in MDS Appendix D-2. The crest length is increased to 36 ft and the top of berm is raised to 2,860.80 ft. The 36-ft length is a practical multiple of the 18-in articulated-block width (24 blocks) and fits along the 195-ft east berm (C-6, p.11). It is selected for reserve: a 30-ft weir would give 1.005206005 ft freeboard at 1.5Q (utilisation 0.995), while 36 ft gives 1.153396722 ft (utilisation 0.867); a longer weir would add crest and basin width without a corresponding benefit. The calculations are:
[48](Normal) H at Q100 = (88.4 / (3.0 × 36))^(2/3) = 0.875022069 ft
[49](Normal) Design WSE at Q100 = 2,858.50 + 0.875022069 = 2,859.375022069 ft
[50](Normal) H at 1.5Q = (132.6 / (3.0 × 36))^(2/3) = 1.146603278 ft
[51](Normal) Design WSE at 1.5Q = 2,858.50 + 1.146603278 = 2,859.646603278 ft
[52](Normal) Freeboard at Q100 = 2,860.80 − 2,859.375022069 = 1.424977931 ft
[53](Normal) Freeboard at 1.5Q = 2,860.80 − 2,859.646603278 = 1.153396722 ft
[54](Normal) The conservative C = 2.6 check also passes: at Q100 the head is 0.962611275 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.462611275 ft, and the freeboard is 1.337388725 ft; at 1.5Q the head is 1.261377607 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.761377607 ft, and the freeboard is 1.038622393 ft. The 100-year freeboard to the new top of berm is 2,860.80 − 2,857.91 = 2.89 ft, and the crest-to-top dimension is 2,860.80 − 2,858.50 = 2.30 ft. Widening the weir alone is not sufficient: at Q100 the 36-ft design WSE of 2,859.375022069 ft is above the existing top of berm of 2,859.20 ft, so the top of berm must be raised to provide freeboard.
[55](Normal) Table 4-1 — Spillway elevation stack (all elevations NAVD 88).
[57](Normal) Table 4-2 — Spillway capacity and freeboard check. The table shows final values rounded to four decimal places; the unrounded values are in the calculation text above.
[59](Normal) For completeness, the 36-ft weir also passes the arithmetic sum of the Phase 3 sub-basin peaks, 96.8 cfs: the head is 0.929610602 ft, the design WSE is 2,859.429610602 ft, and the freeboard to 2,860.80 ft is 1.370389398 ft. The 88.4 cfs timing-adjusted inflow remains the design basis.
[60](Normal) Raising the top of berm by 1.60 ft is feasible within Parcel E. C-6 gives the basin top-of-berm footprint as approximately 293 ft by 195 ft, or 1.31 acres (C-6, p.11). The final map gives Parcel E as 2.04 acres (Final map, Sheet 4, 08/21/2026). With 4H:1V interior and 3H:1V exterior slopes, the top-of-berm footprint expands by roughly 0.15 acre, to about 1.46 acres, which remains inside the 2.04-acre parcel. The berm raise itself fits; the stilling basin, 10-ft riprap and overflow swale must also be shown inside Parcel E or within a drainage easement. The current C-6 does not dimension the east berm margin, so the revised C-6/C-9 must confirm that the 20-ft basin, the riprap and the swale fit. If they do not, the spillway must be shifted or an easement obtained; the basin and swale cannot be built outside Parcel E without an easement. All top-of-berm appurtenances must be raised with the berm, including the outlet headwall (currently top at 2,859.20 ft on C-9, p.18), the access gate and the perimeter maintenance path. The access ramp must remain H-20 capable with a 6-in aggregate base per the C-6 note.
[61](Normal) Before fill placement, the exposed subgrade must be scarified to 8 in, moisture-conditioned to within 2 percent of optimum, and compacted to at least 95% of the ASTM D1557 maximum dry density. The 1.60-ft berm raise must then be engineered fill placed in lifts not exceeding 8 in loose thickness, moisture-conditioned, and compacted to at least 95% of the ASTM D1557 maximum dry density (Geotech Section 6.2, p.8). The revised C-6/C-9 must specify this and the required density testing.
[62](Heading 2) 4.4 Apron and erosion protection
[63](Normal) The existing apron is 15 ft by 20 ft of grouted riprap with D50 = 12 in (C-9, p.17). It has no velocity basis. Using the existing 20-ft weir, the unit discharge at Q100 is 88.4/20 = 4.42 cfs/ft; critical depth is 0.846570029 ft and critical velocity is 5.221068370 ft/s. With a 5.5-ft drop from crest 2,858.50 ft to natural grade 2,853.00 ft, the ideal toe velocity is about 19.530989604 ft/s. For the proposed 36-ft weir, the unit discharge is 2.455555556 cfs/ft, critical depth is 0.572112213 ft, critical velocity is 4.292087285 ft/s, and the toe velocity is still about 19.303419730 ft/s because the drop dominates.
[64](Normal) The Isbash riprap sizing check is:
[65](Normal) D50 = V^2 / [2 · g · C^2 · (Gs − 1)]
[66](Normal) With V = 19.530989604 ft/s, g = 32.2 ft/s^2, C = 0.86 for high turbulence, and Gs = 2.65, the required D50 is 4.853798953 ft, or 58.25 in. Reversing the equation, a 12-in D50 stone is adequate only to about 8.865094247 ft/s. The calculated toe velocity is more than twice that. A 12-in grouted riprap apron cannot be justified by calculation, and increasing the stone to a practical size is not the right solution at this drop. The revised C-9 must use a reinforced concrete stilling basin.
[67](Normal) The minimum acceptable detail is a reinforced concrete stilling basin at least 20 ft long by 36 ft wide, 12 in thick, with baffle blocks and an end sill, keyed 3 ft below grade with cutoff walls at the upstream and downstream ends and weep holes. Downstream of the basin, provide riprap with D50 = 18 in, thickness 27 in (1.5 times D50), 10 ft long by 36 ft wide, over a geotextile filter fabric, keyed into the toe. The drainage lead must demonstrate by calculation that the basin reduces the exit velocity to the riprap allowable velocity; the 18-in D50 is a minimum, not a substitute for the basin design. The downstream riprap and outfall protection must also satisfy the C-6 note reference to Clark County Standard Drawing SD-402.
[68](Heading 1) 5. What the revised C-9 spillway detail must say
[69](Normal) The revised C-9 must replace the current bullet-list detail with a dimensioned spillway plan and section. The following table is the minimum content. Each value is to be shown on the drawing and tied to the calculation sheet. The changed detail and basin notes must be clouded, carry a revision triangle/delta, and be entered in the C-9 revision block; the current title block shows Revision L blank, and the CCPW resubmittal instructions require the revision marking.
[71](Normal) The spillway section must show the upstream and downstream water surfaces, the head H above the crest, the design WSE, the top of berm and the freeboard dimension. It must also show the existing ground at the toe (2,853.00 ft), the stilling basin, the cutoff walls, the riprap and the geotextile. A bullet list without dimensions does not satisfy G-4.
[73](Heading 1) 6. What the revised C-9 basin notes must say
[74](Normal) The current basin notes contain a correct 100-year freeboard statement (1.29 ft) but an incorrect crest offset and no spillway design basis. The notes say the crest is 0.60 ft above the 100-year water surface; the detail says 0.71 ft; the arithmetic is 0.59 ft. The revised notes must replace both numbers with 0.59 ft and must state the spillway design flow, design WSE and freeboard. The following note text is to be carried on revised C-9, with the values shown in the table above.
[76](Normal) The revised notes must not repeat the current 0.60 ft or 0.71 ft crest offset. They must not describe the 100-year freeboard of 1.29 ft as the spillway freeboard. They must not use the 100-year, 24-hour storm as the spillway design flow; that storm governs storage volume, not peak spillway discharge.
[77](Heading 1) 7. Where the overflow goes once it leaves the berm
[78](Normal) The intended overflow path in the current record is: east berm emergency spillway → open swale in Common-Area Parcel E → Windmill Lane gutter line (C-9, Emergency Spillway Detail, p.17). From the Windmill Lane gutter line, the only receiving point of record is the shared outfall at the southwest corner of the parent parcel. The site slopes from the northeast at about 2,905 ft to the southwest outfall at about 2,850 ft (MDS Sections 2.1 and 2.4, p.3–4). The basin outlet is the existing 30-in RCP stub at the southwest corner with invert 2,850.75 ft (C-6, p.11; C-9, p.17), which connects to the CCRFCD regional facility (MDS Section 5.1, p.7; FCD acceptance letter, p.2). The overflow therefore must run west along Windmill Lane to that outfall; it cannot run east away from the only identified receiving point.
[79](Normal) The current record does not demonstrate that path. C-9 has a note, not a plan or profile. There is no swale centerline, invert, width, slope or capacity; no gutter capacity check; and no drainage easement for the overflow across Parcel E. The final map shows a 15-ft drainage easement along the west line of Parcel D, but no overflow easement for Parcel E (Final map, Sheet 3 and Sheet 4, 08/21/2026). The overflow is also not the 30-in principal outlet; the 30-in RCP is the normal basin outlet, not an emergency spillway conduit. Sending 88.4 cfs through the 30-in outlet would be a different design and is not what C-9 shows.
[81](Normal) Our conclusion is that the overflow is intended to end at the shared outfall and the CCRFCD regional facility, but the path is not demonstrated on the current drawings. Until the revised C-9 shows a continuous, positively graded, capacity-checked path within Parcel E and public right-of-way, G-4 cannot be closed. The final map and the drainage narrative must be consistent with that path; if an easement is needed, it must be granted by the final map under Condition 3.

I hereby certify that this Master Drainage Study for Desert Sage Ranch was prepared by me, or under my direct
supervision, and that I am a Professional Engineer duly licensed to practice in the State of Nevada. The
hydrologic and hydraulic methods, criteria and assumptions set forth herein conform to the Clark County
Regional Flood Control District Hydrologic Criteria and Drainage Design Manual applicable at the time of

Jonathan R. Kessler, PE Principal-in-Charge Sundial Engineering & Survey Nevada Professional Engineer No.
14203
(Signed and sealed — original wet seal affixed to record set; cover sheet dated 02/28/2022.)
TABLE OF CONTENTS

Appendices A. Rainfall Depth-Duration Data (CCRFCD) B. Sub-Basin Delineation Maps C. Runoff Computation
Tabulations D. Storage-Indication Routing Output E. Phasing Exhibit — 24×36 sheet, reduced F. CCRFCD
Acceptance Correspondence
1. INTRODUCTION AND PROJECT DESCRIPTION
1.1 Purpose
The purpose of this Master Drainage Study is to establish the hydrologic and hydraulic basis of design for storm
drainage improvements serving the Desert Sage Ranch subdivision, a 140-acre residential development to be
constructed in three phases in the Enterprise area of unincorporated Clark County, Nevada. This study is
submitted to the Clark County Regional Flood Control District (CCRFCD) for acceptance and, upon acceptance,
is intended to serve as the master planning document governing all subsequent improvement plan submittals for
the individual phases.
1.2 Project Location
Desert Sage Ranch occupies a portion of Section 27, Township 22 South, Range 60 East, M.D.M., in
unincorporated Clark County. The site is bounded generally by Rainbow Boulevard on the west and Windmill
Lane on the south, with the project address of record identified as Rainbow Boulevard and Windmill Lane, Las
Vegas, Nevada 89178. Assessor Parcel Number 177-27-201-001 encompasses the balance of the site not
already partitioned.
The site is located within the Enterprise Town Advisory Board area of unincorporated Clark County and is
governed by Clark County Code Title 30. Land use planning oversight is exercised by Clark County
Comprehensive Planning.
1.3 Site Description and Development
The 140-acre site is generally undeveloped desert terrain sloping gently from the northeast to the southwest at
an average grade of approximately 1.6 percent. Native ground cover consists of sparse creosote and bursage
on gravelly, well-drained soils overlying a caliche-influenced subsurface typical of the Enterprise sub-basin.
There are no defined natural watercourses across the site; historic runoff sheet-flows to the southwest.
Desert Sage Ranch will be developed as a single-family residential subdivision served by public streets. Phase
3 consists of 60 half-acre lots (100 ft × 220 ft, approximately 22,000 sf); Phases 1 and 2 consist of smaller
residential lots (approximately 6,050 sf, 55 ft × 110 ft) per the recorded Phase 1-2 Final Map. The full 140 acres
will be built out in three sequential phases:
• Phase 1 — 45.0 acres, northern portion of the site.
• Phase 2 — 55.0 acres, central portion of the site.
• Phase 3 — 40.0 acres, southern portion of the site, comprising 60 half-acre lots and associated street
frontage, HOA common-area park and streetscape improvements.
Each phase will be constructed under its own improvement plan set, prepared to be consistent with this Master
Drainage Study.


--- page 3 ---
1.4 Regulatory Framework
This study has been prepared in conformance with:
• Clark County Regional Flood Control District Hydrologic Criteria and Drainage Design Manual, edition
applicable at the time of preparation;
• Clark County Uniform Standard Drawings and applicable Public Works standards;
• Clark County Code Title 30 (development standards).
Hydrologic and hydraulic methods, precipitation input, loss rates and detention criteria are drawn from the
CCRFCD manual as it stood at the time of study preparation and acceptance. Subsequent phase-level design
shall comply with the master allocations set forth herein.
1.5 Study Deliverables
This document establishes:
• Design storm criteria and rainfall depths.
• Tributary-area delineation for the full 140 acres, broken down by development phase.
• Peak discharge estimates for the tributary sub-basins under fully developed conditions.
• A shared onsite detention approach with a fixed allocation of storage volume to each phase.
• Allowance for the full 140 acres at a shared outfall to the downstream regional facility, with a maximum
permitted discharge.
• A phasing exhibit identifying phase boundaries and detention basin locations.
2. EXISTING CONDITIONS AND OFFSITE TRIBUTARY
2.1 Topography and Soils
Existing topography across the 140-acre site is a gently sloping desert plain. Elevations range from
approximately 2,905 feet at the northeast corner to approximately 2,850 feet at the southwest outfall point,
yielding an average site slope of approximately 1.6 percent to the southwest.
Surface soils across the site are classified as SM to SP-SM (silty sands and poorly graded sands with silt), with
cemented caliche horizons at variable depth. Infiltration rates in the caliche zone are low, and no percolation
credit is taken in the hydrologic analysis. The full computed runoff volume is treated as surface flow for the
purposes of this study.
2.2 Existing Drainage Pattern
Under existing conditions, stormwater sheet-flows overland from north-northeast to south-southwest across the
site. There are no defined channels within the property boundaries. At the southwest corner of the site, runoff


--- page 4 ---
historically discharges toward the downstream regional drainage facility maintained by CCRFCD.
2.3 Offsite Tributary from the North
The site accepts a modest offsite drainage flow entering along the northern boundary of what will become Phase
1. The offsite tributary area upstream of the north boundary consists of approximately 38 acres of low-density
residential and open desert land. Under fully developed offsite conditions consistent with the surrounding land
use plan, the offsite peak inflow at the northern site boundary has been estimated as summarized in Section 3
and Appendix C.
The offsite tributary flow enters the site as sheet flow along the northern boundary and, at build-out, will be
conveyed through the Phase 1 street network to the shared onsite detention basin(s). No offsite bypass channel
is proposed; the accepted offsite flow is passed through the onsite storm drain and routed through detention
along with the onsite runoff.
2.4 Downstream Conveyance
The shared onsite outfall is located at the southwest corner of the property and discharges to the downstream
regional CCRFCD facility via an existing reinforced concrete pipe stub set during earlier regional construction.
The receiving facility has been reviewed against the shared outfall allowance identified in Section 5; downstream
capacity is not the controlling constraint for the site's release rate. The controlling constraint is the outfall
allowance established for Desert Sage Ranch and set forth in this study.
3. HYDROLOGY
3.1 Design Storm
Design storm criteria applied in this study are drawn from the CCRFCD Hydrologic Criteria and Drainage Design
Manual applicable at the time of preparation. The following storms have been evaluated:
• 100-year, 6-hour storm — used for peak discharge estimation and storm drain sizing.
• 100-year, 24-hour storm — used for detention basin sizing (governing storage volume).

3.2 Method
Rainfall-runoff modeling was performed using CCRFCD-accepted methods appropriate for a subdivision of this
size, applying the Green-Ampt infiltration approach for pervious surfaces and directly-connected impervious

Routing to and through the shared detention basin(s) was performed using the storage-indication method.
Impervious cover assumed at build-out reflects the approved half-acre residential lot type with associated street
and driveway coverage, streetscape landscape strips, and HOA common-area park.
3.3 Tributary Area Breakdown by Phase
The 140-acre site drains as a single system to the shared outfall, but for the purposes of allocating detention
storage the site is subdivided into three phase-based tributary areas that correspond to the phased development

provided in Appendix C.
3.4 Peak Discharge Summary — Fully Developed Conditions
Fully developed peak flows to the shared onsite detention basin(s), computed under the 100-year, 6-hour storm
inclusive of the accepted offsite tributary inflow at the northern boundary, are summarized in Appendix C. The
peak inflow at the shared basin(s) governs the storm drain sizing but does not govern the shared outfall release,
which is fixed by the allowance in Section 5.
4. DETENTION SIZING
4.1 Shared Onsite Detention Approach
Desert Sage Ranch is served by a shared onsite detention approach: the detention volume required to attenuate
the site's peak discharge to the accepted outfall release rate is provided in shared onsite detention facilities


--- page 6 ---
constructed as the subdivision phases advance. Detention basin locations are identified on the phasing exhibit
(Section 6).
The shared approach avoids duplication of small phase-scale basins and consolidates operations and
maintenance for the HOA. Because the phases share the same outfall and downstream facility, the storage
requirement has been determined for the fully developed 140-acre site and then allocated among the three
phases in accordance with the acreage and impervious cover of each phase.
4.2 Governing Design Storm
Storage sizing is governed by the 100-year, 24-hour design storm. The 100-year, 6-hour storm is used to check
peak discharge to the shared basin(s) and storm drain sizing, but does not govern storage. Storage-indication
routing under the 100-year, 24-hour storm, with the outfall released at the allowance identified in Section 5,
produces a total site-wide required storage volume of 16.4 acre-feet.
4.3 Detention Allocation by Phase
Total storage required for the fully developed 140-acre site is allocated to the three phases on the basis of
tributary runoff volume and position in the shared outfall, not by pro-rata acreage. Phase 3 discharges last
and carries the largest attenuation duty; volumes were reviewed and fixed at District acceptance, and are
the fixed planning basis for subsequent phase-level submittals.

4.4 Fixed at Acceptance
The detention allocation established in Table 4-1 has been sized to reflect the tributary area, phase acreage and
assumed impervious cover of each phase at the time of study preparation. The allocations shown are set at the
time of District acceptance of this study and are not to be adjusted absent formal amendment.
Any proposed change to the detention allocation for any phase — whether by revision of tributary area,
impervious assumption, hydrologic methodology or storage-indication input — constitutes a change to the


--- page 7 ---
accepted allocation and shall be processed as a formal amendment to this Master Drainage Study, submitted to
the Clark County Regional Flood Control District for re-review and re-acceptance in accordance with Section 7.
5. OUTFALL
5.1 Shared Outfall
The full 140-acre Desert Sage Ranch subdivision discharges to the downstream regional CCRFCD facility
through a single shared outfall located at the southwest corner of the site. The outfall discharges via an existing
reinforced concrete pipe stub previously installed by others as part of regional drainage construction.
Confirmation of downstream capacity has been obtained from the District as part of this study's review.
5.2 Allowance and Cap
An allowance for the full 140 acres at the shared outfall to the downstream regional facility has been established
for Desert Sage Ranch, subject to the following cap:
Q100 ≤ 78 cfs at the shared outfall.
The 78 cfs cap represents the maximum permitted 100-year peak discharge from the fully developed 140-acre
site into the receiving regional facility. Storage-indication routing through the shared onsite detention basin(s) as
sized in Section 4 attenuates the fully developed peak inflow at the basin(s) to a peak release at or below the 78
cfs cap.
5.3 Application to Phase-Level Plans
Because the cap applies to the shared outfall for the full 140-acre site — not to any single phase — phase-level
improvement plan sets are not to compute a phase-specific outfall discharge. Each phase's contribution is
routed into the shared detention system, and the shared outfall discharge remains subject to the 78 cfs cap at
build-out.
6. PHASING EXHIBIT
The Phasing Exhibit, provided as Appendix E and reproduced at reduced scale below, identifies:
• The three phase boundaries — Phase 1 (northern), Phase 2 (central), and Phase 3 (southern) —
comprising the 140-acre site.
• The location of the shared onsite detention basin(s) serving the subdivision.
• The offsite tributary corridor along the northern site boundary.
• The shared outfall at the southwest corner of the site and its connection to the downstream regional
CCRFCD facility.
• The phase-boundary storm drain interconnections that link each phase's contributory area to the shared
detention system.


--- page 8 ---
The exhibit is drawn at 1"=200′ on a 24×36 sheet; reference should be made to the full-size exhibit in Appendix
E for construction of phase-level improvement plans. Phase-level plans shall reflect the boundaries and basin
locations shown on the exhibit; deviations require formal amendment as set forth in Section 7.
(Phasing Exhibit — see Appendix E.)
7. CONCLUSION
7.1 Summary
This Master Drainage Study establishes the hydrologic and hydraulic basis of design for the 140-acre Desert
Sage Ranch subdivision. The study:
• adopts the 100-year, 6-hour and 100-year, 24-hour design storms in accordance with the CCRFCD
Hydrologic Criteria and Drainage Design Manual applicable at time of preparation;
• delineates tributary areas for the full 140 acres, broken down by the three development phases;
• establishes a shared onsite detention approach with fixed volume allocations by phase — Phase 1 at 4.2
acre-feet, Phase 2 at 5.8 acre-feet, Phase 3 at 6.4 acre-feet, and total site at 16.4 acre-feet;
• confirms an allowance for the full 140 acres at the shared outfall to the downstream regional facility,
capped at Q100 = 78 cfs;
• provides a phasing exhibit identifying phase boundaries, detention basin locations, offsite tributary corridor
and shared outfall.
7.2 Basis for Subsequent Design
Upon CCRFCD acceptance, this Master Drainage Study serves as the master planning document for all
subsequent improvement plan submittals for Desert Sage Ranch, including but not limited to Phase 1, Phase 2
and Phase 3 grading and drainage plan sets and their supporting hydrology, storm drain and detention
worksheets. Phase-level design shall be consistent with the tributary breakdown, detention allocation by phase,
and shared outfall allowance identified herein.
7.3 Amendments
Changes to the accepted detention allocations set forth in Table 4-1, the outfall allowance set forth in Section 5,
or the tributary breakdown and phase boundaries set forth in Sections 3 and 6, require formal amendment to this
study and re-review by the Clark County Regional Flood Control District. Phase-level improvement plans that
propose to depart from the accepted allocations or allowance shall be preceded by an accepted amendment; no
phase-level plan set shall be approved on the basis of a departure that has not been separately submitted to
and accepted by the District.
The CCRFCD acceptance letter dated February 28, 2022 (Appendix F) confirms this requirement and is
incorporated herein by reference.

Dear Applicant:
Recital of the Request
Callaway Land Partners has filed application TM-22-500041 seeking tentative map approval for the residential
subdivision known as Desert Sage Ranch, comprising 140 acres to be developed in three phases in the
Enterprise planning area of unincorporated Clark County. As presented, the tentative map lays out a total
build-out of the subdivision with the final 40-acre phase (Phase 3) proposed for sixty (60) half-acre single-family
residential lots served by internal public rights-of-way, a shared detention facility, a homeowners association
park parcel, and streetscape improvements consistent with the approved land use designation.
The tentative map was reviewed by the Enterprise Town Advisory Board on the date noted in the record, by staff
of this Department, and by the reviewing agencies identified below. The application was heard by the Clark
County Planning Commission on this date.
Findings
Based on the record before it, and after receiving the recommendation of staff and the recommendation of the
Enterprise Town Advisory Board, the Planning Commission finds that:
The tentative map substantially conforms to the requirements of Chapter 30 of the Clark County Code (Title
30 — Unified Development Code) applicable to the property, subject to the conditions of approval set forth
herein.
The proposed subdivision is consistent with the goals and objectives of the adopted Enterprise Land Use
Plan and the Clark County Comprehensive Master Plan.
Public services and facilities, including water, sewer, storm drainage, fire protection, and access, are or can
be made available to serve the subdivision at the densities and configurations shown, subject to the
conditions herein.
The applicant has demonstrated the ability to comply with Nevada Revised Statutes ("NRS") Chapter 278,
including but not limited to NRS 278.360, quoted below.
Approval


--- page 2 ---
Based on the foregoing findings, the tentative map identified as TM-22-500041, Desert Sage Ranch is hereby
APPROVED, subject to the thirty-one (31) numbered conditions set forth on the pages that follow. Compliance
with each condition is a prerequisite to any subsequent action of this Department or any other reviewing agency,
including improvement plan approval and final map recordation. Conditions are grouped by the department that
imposed them. The full set is binding regardless of grouping.
Statutory Presentation Requirements
The applicant's attention is directed to NRS 278.360, which governs the presentation of final maps in a phased
subdivision, the substance of which is summarised below:
"A final map presented for recordation as the first map in a series must be presented to the
governing body within four (4) years after the date of approval or conditional approval of the tentative
map. Each successive final map in the same series must be presented within two (2) years after the
date on which the immediately preceding final map is recorded. Failure to timely present a map
terminates all proceedings relating to the subdivision. The governing body may, upon written
application filed after the applicable period has expired, grant an extension of not more than two (2)
years."
The applicant is on notice that the four-year and two-year periods described above run from the events identified
in the statute, not from any calendar reference stated by staff. Extensions of not more than two (2) years may be
sought only by written application filed after the applicable period has expired, and are discretionary with the
governing body. Nothing in this letter, and no informal communication from staff, shall be construed to extend,
waive, or modify the statutory deadlines.
CONDITIONS OF APPROVAL
A. Public Works — Development Review (Conditions 1 through 10)
Improvement plans for all phases shall be prepared by a professional engineer registered in the State of
Nevada in accordance with the Clark County Uniform Standard Specifications and Drawings for Public
Works Construction and the Clark County Design and Construction Standards, current edition at the time of
submittal.
A drainage study, prepared in accordance with the Clark County Regional Flood Control District Hydrologic
Criteria and Drainage Design Manual, shall be submitted with the first improvement plan submittal for each
phase and shall demonstrate conformance with all applicable accepted district studies. Any proposed
deviation from district-accepted parameters shall be resubmitted for district re-review prior to improvement
plan approval.
Right-of-way dedications and easements shown on the tentative map, including all public utility easements,
drainage easements, and non-vehicular access easements, shall be granted by the recorded final map for
the phase in which the affected area lies.
Full half-street improvements shall be constructed along all abutting collector and arterial streets adjacent to
the phase being platted, including curb, gutter, sidewalk, pavement, streetlights, signing and striping, in
accordance with the applicable cross-section.


--- page 3 ---
Internal streets shall be constructed to Clark County local-street standards. Cul-de-sac dimensions,
knuckles, and turning radii shall satisfy the requirements of both Public Works and the Clark County Fire
Department.
Sight visibility triangles shall be shown on the improvement plans and the landscape plans at every
intersection and driveway. Landscaping, signage, and walls within the sight visibility zone shall comply with
Section 30.52.025 (Sight Zones) of the Clark County Code.
A traffic impact analysis shall be provided at the improvement plan stage for any phase, or portion of a
phase, whose lot count, trip generation, or access configuration differs from the assumptions used in the
tentative map traffic study. Off-site mitigation, if warranted, shall be constructed or bonded as a condition of
the applicable final map.
Prior to recordation of any final map, the applicant shall furnish a performance bond, cash-in-lieu, or other
security acceptable to the Director of Public Works in the full amount of the engineer's estimate of probable
cost of the public improvements associated with that phase.
Final acceptance of public improvements for each phase shall be by written notice of acceptance from the
Director of Public Works following completion of the two-year maintenance period and the punch-list walk.
Bond release, in whole or in part, shall be governed by the terms of the applicable security instrument and
shall not occur automatically.
Construction stormwater discharges shall be authorized under the current Nevada Department of
Environmental Protection general permit (NVR100000) prior to the commencement of grading. A Notice of
Intent shall be filed and a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan implemented for the duration of
construction, and a Notice of Termination shall be filed upon final stabilization.
B. Clark County Fire Department (Conditions 11 through 13)
Fire apparatus access roads, hydrant locations, hydrant flow, and required fire flow shall be shown on the
improvement plans and shall comply with the International Fire Code as amended and adopted by Clark
County. Secondary emergency access shall be provided in accordance with the Fire Code, and any
secondary access designated as temporary shall be identified as such on the plans with the expiration event
stated.
Water mains and appurtenances serving fire hydrants shall be operational and accepted, and required fire
flow shall be demonstrated by flow test, prior to combustible construction on any lot within the affected
phase.
Street names, address ranges, and access gate details (if any) shall be submitted for Fire Department
review concurrently with the improvement plan submittal. Access codes to any gates restricting emergency
access shall be provided to the Clark County Fire Department and the Metropolitan Police Department prior
to activation.
C. Comprehensive Planning (Conditions 14 through 20)
Any significant change to approved plans, including but not limited to landscape and streetscape
treatments in common areas, shall be subject to design review as a public hearing before the
applicable Town Advisory Board and Planning Commission prior to staff-level action.
The final map(s) shall conform to the tentative map as approved, including lot count, lot geometry, phase
boundaries, public street alignments, common-area boundaries, and dedications. Modification to any of the


--- page 4 ---
foregoing at the final map stage that is not the result of a routine survey adjustment shall be treated as a
significant change under Condition 14.
Covenants, Conditions and Restrictions (CC&Rs) establishing a homeowners association, defining
common-area maintenance obligations, and identifying the party responsible for ongoing maintenance of
streetscapes, park parcels, entry features, walls, and drainage facilities not accepted by the County, shall be
recorded concurrently with the final map for the applicable phase. A common-area maintenance exhibit shall
be attached to the CC&Rs.
All identification signage, entry monumentation, and community features shall be shown on the landscape
plans and shall be subject to Comprehensive Planning review prior to installation. Off-premise signage is
not authorized by this approval.
Lighting on streetscape, park parcels, and entry features shall be full cut-off and shall comply with the
outdoor lighting standards of the Clark County Code. Photometric plans shall be provided with the
improvement plan submittal for common-area lighting.
Model home complexes, sales trailers, and temporary construction offices are not authorized by this
approval. Separate permits shall be obtained through this Department prior to the establishment of any such
use.
This approval does not vest zoning, use, or development standards beyond those in effect on the date of
approval. Nothing herein exempts the applicant from compliance with subsequently adopted regulations that
apply to actions taken after the effective date of those regulations, including but not limited to landscape and
water conservation standards.
D. Utilities (Conditions 21 through 24)
A will-serve letter from the Las Vegas Valley Water District for domestic water and fire flow service to the
phase being platted shall be current at the time of final map recordation. The applicant shall be responsible
for maintaining currency of the will-serve; a lapsed will-serve shall be re-issued prior to recordation.
A capacity confirmation from the Clark County Water Reclamation District for wastewater collection and
treatment capacity for the phase being platted shall be current at the time of final map recordation. Sewer
capacity confirmations are issued by the District under a separate schedule from water will-serve letters and
are subject to their own expiration terms; the applicant is responsible for verifying currency independently.
Dry utility joint-trench alignment shall be coordinated with the electric, natural gas, and telecommunications
purveyors. A composite dry utility plan shall be submitted with the improvement plans, and joint trench
easements shown on the final map shall reflect the composite plan as coordinated.
Backflow prevention, meter sizing, and cross-connection control shall comply with the requirements of the
Las Vegas Valley Water District and the Southern Nevada Health District.
E. Landscape (Conditions 25 through 28)
Landscape and irrigation plans shall be prepared by a landscape architect registered in the State of Nevada
and shall comply with Title 30, Chapter 30.64 (Site Landscape and Screening Standards) of the Clark
County Code, including the street frontage tree standard, plant palette, and turf restrictions in effect at the
time of submittal.


--- page 5 ---
Streetscapes and medians shall be planted with low-water, climate-adapted plant material in accordance
with the Southern Nevada Water Authority regional plant list. Turf shall not be installed within any
streetscape, median, or right-of-way, nor within ten (10) feet of any street or curb.
Landscape plans for any phase proposing turf shall comply with all applicable Title 30 turf-placement
standards in effect at the time of the landscape submittal. Documentation supporting compliance shall
accompany the landscape submittal.
An irrigation demand worksheet shall be submitted with the landscape plans, showing water application
rates by irrigation method, area by hydrozone, and total annual demand. The worksheet shall be updated to
reflect any revision to the planting palette prior to landscape approval.
F. Other Reviewing Agencies (Conditions 29 through 31)
Southern Nevada Health District: Approval of the sanitary sewer connection to the regional system, and of
any private on-site treatment, shall be obtained prior to combustible construction. The Health District's
certificate shall appear on the recorded final map.
Clark County Recorder / Clark County Surveyor: The final map shall be prepared in accordance with NRS
278.010 through 278.630 and the map checklist of the Clark County Surveyor. The Recorder's note required
by NRS 278.5695 (examination of subsequent changes by reference to the cumulative index) shall appear on Sheet 1.
Nevada Division of Water Resources: The Division's approval shall appear on the final map for each phase.
Statutory Presentation Deadlines (Reminder)
As stated above under Statutory Presentation Requirements, the first final map in the series must be presented
within four (4) years after the date of approval or conditional approval of the tentative map, and each
successive final map in the same series must be presented within two (2) years after the date on which the
immediately preceding final map is recorded. Failure to timely present a map terminates all proceedings
relating to the subdivision. An extension of not more than two (2) years may be granted only upon written
application filed after the applicable period has expired. The applicant is directed to compute its own
presentation deadlines from the operative events identified in NRS 278.360.
Notice of Appeal
Any person aggrieved by this decision may appeal to the Clark County Board of County Commissioners by filing
a written notice of appeal with the Department of Comprehensive Planning within ten (10) calendar days of the
date of this letter. Appeals must be accompanied by the applicable fee. If no appeal is filed within the ten-day
period, this decision becomes final.

Notes issued: 06/23/2026

Max Braddock | Sundial Engineering & Survey | Project Manager | In person
